name: MarketMan
tagline: Back-of-house inventory, purchasing, invoice capture and food cost tracking for restaurants.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The math at the heart of MarketMan is not hard: items with units, recipes with yields, counts at the start and end of a period, invoices in, theoretical usage versus actual, variance report. An agent can build that in a weekend and a single-kitchen operator will get real COGS numbers out of it. What it cannot hand you is the plumbing: POS sales feeds so theoretical usage is automatic, supplier catalogs and order transmission, invoice OCR that survives a crumpled vendor PDF, and QuickBooks or Xero sync. Without those, someone types invoices in by hand every week, which is exactly the chore people buy this to stop doing. Worth building if you run one site and like spreadsheets; not worth building if you have four sites and a chef who will not use it.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you keep items, vendors, recipes and par levels, enter invoices and physical counts, and get period COGS plus theoretical-versus-actual variance per item.
requirements: Node 20+ and a machine to run it on
Somebody willing to key in invoices manually, or a CSV from the supplier
A starting item list with units and pack sizes
Sales data export from the POS if you want theoretical usage
whatYouLose: POS integrations that pull item-level sales so theoretical usage updates itself
Invoice OCR and vendor price-change alerts, so every invoice is hand entry
Supplier catalogs and real purchase orders sent to the vendor, not a PDF you email yourself
Accounting sync to QuickBooks or Xero, and the multi-location roll-ups
A mobile counting app that works offline in a walk-in with no signal
moatNotes: The defensible parts are the POS and accounting connectors plus years of vendor catalog and price history, not the inventory math.
whyPeopleStillPay: Restaurant operators do not pay for variance arithmetic, they pay for the data arriving without anyone typing it. Toast or Square sales flowing in nightly, invoices parsed from a photo, vendor prices tracked so you notice chicken went up 14 percent, orders actually reaching the supplier, and the whole thing landing in the accountant's ledger. Each of those is a separate integration with its own certification, credentials and edge cases, and a kitchen has no appetite for maintaining any of it. A DIY build is fine for one owner-operator who already does counts; it collapses the moment the process depends on a line cook remembering to enter something.
notes: The inventory ledger is a weekend; the invoice pipeline is the product.
prompt:
Build a local-first restaurant inventory and food cost app for a single location. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Next.js 15 App Router with TypeScript
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/inventory.db
- Drizzle ORM for schema and migrations
- Tailwind CSS, plain server actions, no external UI kit
- Runs with `npm run dev` on localhost only

Data model:
- items: name, category, base unit (g, ml, each), pack size, pack cost, vendor, par level, storage location
- vendors: name, contact, order email
- recipes: name, yield quantity and unit, lines referencing items or other recipes with quantities
- menu_items: name, sell price, linked recipe
- invoices: vendor, date, lines (item, quantity, pack cost), auto-updates item latest cost and keeps price history
- counts: date, label (opening or closing), lines (item, counted quantity in base unit)
- sales_imports: date range plus rows of menu_item and quantity sold, from CSV

Screens:
1. Items list with search, inline edit, current cost per base unit
2. Recipe editor showing computed cost per yield and cost per portion, plus margin against sell price
3. Invoice entry form, fast keyboard-first, with a price-change warning when a pack cost moves more than 10 percent
4. Count sheet grouped by storage location, printable, enterable on a phone browser
5. Period report: pick two counts, get opening value, purchases, closing value, actual usage and COGS in dollars and as a percent of sales
6. Variance report: theoretical usage from the sales CSV and recipes versus actual usage from counts, per item, sorted by dollar impact
7. Order suggestions: items below par, grouped by vendor, exportable as CSV or a plain-text email body

Also: CSV import and export for items, invoices and counts. Seed script with about 40 realistic items and 6 recipes.

Explicitly out of scope: invoice OCR, POS API integrations, accounting sync, multi-location, user roles, payments. Put any config in .env.example. Write a README with setup, the COGS formula used, and a one-paragraph note on what this does not do.
